title: Microbial Metabolism I: Catabolic Reactions
lead: for ATP synthesis If you look at the cell, you see three items: matter, energy, and space. Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. Soil, water, and air are matters. Energy is matter or its transferable properties that lack mass and do not occupy any space, yet it can move and change the state of matter (solid to liquid or gas) and move it. Light, heat, electromagnetic energy, sound, and chemical bonds are forms of energy. Space is a boundless three-dimensional expanse where matter (and energy) exists. Matter, energy, and space are everywhere, including the cell. Then what about life? No one will ever know (because, deep down, all of this is unreal and probabilistic), but there are some assumptions about life. NASA defines life as a self-sustaining chemical system, the cell, that can transform energy (convert one form of energy to another), maintain homeostasis (able to keep some conditions relatively stable), replicate (the genome to create progeny), mutate (survive despite some changes to the nucleotide sequence of the genome), and evolve (thrive with sufficiently different nucleotide sequences of the genome). Each of these is accomplished through chemical reactions. Thus, life is a series of controlled chemical reactions. A chemical reaction is a process that breaks and/or creates strong chemical bonds, such as covalent and ionic bonds. Note that breaking or making weak bonds (hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces) is not considered a chemical reaction. Note the chemical reaction between two chemical compounds A-B and C-D, below: A-B + C-D à A-C + B-D This chemical reaction broke bonds between A and B and between C and D, then formed bonds between A and C and between B and D. It is estimated that the cell conducts about one billion chemical reactions every second. How many different chemical reactions occur in the lifetime of a cell is unfathomable. The totality of the chemical reactions in the cell is metabolic reactions. A microbiologist should have a strong understanding of microbial metabolism because this knowledge helps manipulate microbial growth and develop new products and services from microbial activities.

blocks.text: The metabolic reactions that break larger molecules into smaller ones and into atoms are catabolic reactions, and the phenomenon is called catabolism. Breaking down polysaccharides into simple sugars, and simple sugars into CO2 and water, are catabolic reactions (Fig. 4.1). Chemical reactions that involve the synthesis of larger molecules from smaller molecules and atoms are anabolic (or biosynthetic) reactions, and the phenomenon is anabolism. The synthesis of glucose from water and CO2, and the synthesis of proteins from amino acids, are anabolic reactions (Fig. 4.1).

Chemical bonds are a form of potential energy (energy due to the position and orientation of atoms). The catabolic reactions break and/or reorganize chemical bonds. When broken, chemical bonds release energy. The released energy may dissipate as heat energy, or it can be used to form new chemical bonds, creating molecules and chemical compounds.
Fig. 4.1. Catabolic and anabolic reactions and ATP. A. Catabolic and anabolic reactions are coupled. A molecule

of glycogen is broken into glucose, and glucose molecules are broken down to CO2 and H2O. Some of the energy released by these catabolic reactions is conserved as ATP. ATP is then used to conduct anabolic reactions, such as protein synthesis. The green arrows indicate the catabolic reactions, and the red arrows indicate the anabolic reactions. B. Structure of ATP. Because the -PO4 groups of ATP are negatively charged, they repel each other, placing strains on the covalent bonds (indicated by the arrows) and making them relatively unstable. One of these two bonds can be broken easily, releasing about 7.3 kcal/mol of energy.

A chemical compound is called a high-energy compound if it contains one or more high-energy covalent bonds. High-energy covalent bonds are relatively weak covalent bonds that, when broken, release energy. One such high- energy compound is ATP (Fig. 4.1).

Energy released by many catabolic reactions is stored in ATP (Fig. 4.1). Chloroplasts and photosynthetic bacteria harvest solar energy and store some of it in ATP. High-energy compounds, including ATP, are unstable because they have weak/unstable high-energy covalent bonds.

Anabolic reactions create new chemical bonds, but they may require energy. The energy for the anabolic (biosynthetic) reactions comes from high-energy chemical compounds such as ATP. Since high-energy chemical compounds are quite unstable, anabolic and catabolic reactions are generally coupled (Fig. 4.1). If the anabolic and the catabolic reactions were not coupled, the energy released by catabolic reactions would dissipate as heat. This and the next chapter (Chapter 5) discuss bioenergetics, the process of energy transformation (i.e., ATP synthesis and the use of ATP energy for anabolic reactions) in the cell. However, before that, we will make a rough inventory of the cell's chemicals (to make it more relevant to metabolism) and investigate why chemical reactions occur.

blocks.text: The term used to describe all of the chemical reactions inside a cell is metabolism (Figure 8.2). Cellular processes such as the building or breaking down of complex molecules occur through series of stepwise, interconnected chemical reactions called metabolic pathways. Reactions that are spontaneous and release energy are exergonic reactions, whereas endergonic reactions require energy to proceed. The term anabolism refers to those endergonic metabolic pathways involved in biosynthesis, converting simple molecular building blocks into more complex molecules, and fueled by the use of cellular energy. Conversely, the term catabolism refers to exergonic pathways that break down complex molecules into simpler ones. Molecular energy stored in the bonds of complex molecules is released in catabolic pathways and harvested in such a way that it can be used to produce high-energy molecules, which are used to drive anabolic pathways. Thus, in terms of energy and molecules, cells are continually balancing catabolism with anabolism.
Figure 8.2 Metabolism includes catabolism and anabolism. Anabolic pathways require energy to synthesize larger
molecules. Catabolic pathways generate energy by breaking down larger molecules. Both types of pathways are required for maintaining the cell’s energy balance.
Classification by Carbon and Energy Source

Organisms can be identified according to the source of carbon they use for metabolism as well as their energy source. The prefixes auto- (“self”) and hetero- (“other”) refer to the origins of the carbon sources various organisms can use. Organisms that convert inorganic carbon dioxide (CO 2) into organic carbon compounds are autotrophs. Plants and cyanobacteria are well-known examples of autotrophs. Conversely, heterotrophs rely on more complex organic carbon compounds as nutrients; these are provided to them initially by autotrophs. Many organisms, ranging from humans to many prokaryotes, including the well-studied Escherichia coli, are heterotrophic.

Organisms can also be identified by the energy source they use. All energy is derived from the transfer of electrons, but the source of electrons differs between various types of organisms. The prefixes photo- (“light”) and chemo- (“chemical”) refer to the energy sources that various organisms use. Those that get their energy for electron transfer from light are phototrophs, whereas chemotrophs obtain energy for electron transfer by breaking chemical bonds. There are two types of chemotrophs: organotrophs and lithotrophs. Organotrophs, including humans, fungi, and many prokaryotes, are chemotrophs that obtain energy from organic compounds. Lithotrophs (“litho” means “rock”) are chemotrophs that get energy from inorganic compounds, including hydrogen sulfide (H 2S) and reduced iron. Lithotrophy is unique to the microbial world.

The strategies used to obtain both carbon and energy can be combined for the classification of organisms according to nutritional type. Most organisms are chemoheterotrophs because they use organic molecules as both their electron and carbon sources. Table 8.1 summarizes this and the other classifications.

Oxidation and Reduction in Metabolism

The transfer of electrons between molecules is important because most of the energy stored in atoms and used to fuel cell functions is in the form of high-energy electrons. The transfer of energy in the form of electrons allows the cell to transfer and use energy incrementally; that is, in small packages rather than a single, destructive burst. Reactions that remove electrons from donor molecules, leaving them oxidized, are oxidation reactions; those that add electrons to acceptor molecules, leaving them reduced, are reduction reactions. Because electrons can move from one molecule to another, oxidation and reduction occur in tandem. These pairs of reactions are called oxidation-reduction reactions, or redox reactions.

Energy Carriers: NAD + , NADP + , FAD, and ATP The energy released from the breakdown of the chemical bonds within nutrients can be stored either through the reduction of electron carriers or in the bonds of adenosine triphosphate (ATP). In living systems, a small class of compounds functions as mobile electron carriers, molecules that bind to and shuttle high-energy electrons between compounds in pathways. The principal electron carriers we will consider originate from the B vitamin group and are derivatives of nucleotides; they are nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, nicotine adenine dinucleotide phosphate, and flavin adenine dinucleotide. These compounds can be easily reduced or oxidized. Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD +/NADH) is the most common mobile electron carrier used in catabolism. NAD + is the oxidized form of the molecule; NADH is the reduced form of the molecule. Nicotine adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP +), the oxidized form of an NAD + variant that contains an extra phosphate group, is another important electron carrier; it forms NADPH when reduced. The oxidized form of flavin adenine dinucleotide is FAD, and its reduced form is FADH 2. Both NAD +/NADH and FAD/FADH 2 are extensively used in energy extraction from sugars during catabolism in chemoheterotrophs, whereas NADP +/NADPH plays an important role in anabolic reactions and photosynthesis. Collectively, FADH 2, NADH, and NADPH are often referred to as having reducing power due to their ability to donate electrons to various chemical reactions.

A living cell must be able to handle the energy released during catabolism in a way that enables the cell to store energy safely and release it for use only as needed. Living cells accomplish this by using the compound adenosine triphosphate (ATP). ATP is often called the “energy currency” of the cell, and, like currency, this versatile compound can be used to fill any energy need of the cell. At the heart of ATP is a molecule of adenosine monophosphate (AMP), which is composed of an adenine molecule bonded to a ribose molecule and a single phosphate group. Ribose is a five-carbon sugar found in RNA, and AMP is one of the nucleotides in RNA. The addition of a second phosphate group to this core molecule results in the formation of adenosine diphosphate (ADP); the addition of a third phosphate group forms ATP (Figure 8.3). Adding a phosphate group to a molecule, a process called phosphorylation, requires energy. Phosphate groups are negatively charged and thus repel one another when they are arranged in series, as they are in ADP and ATP. This repulsion makes the ADP and ATP molecules inherently unstable. Thus, the bonds between phosphate groups (one in ADP and two in ATP) are called high-energy phosphate bonds. When these high- energy bonds are broken to release one phosphate (called inorganic phosphate [Pi]) or two connected phosphate groups (called pyrophosphate [PP i]) from ATP through a process called dephosphorylation, energy is released to drive endergonic reactions (Figure 8.4).
Figure 8.3 The energy released from dephosphorylation of ATP is used to drive cellular work, including anabolic
pathways. ATP is regenerated through phosphorylation, harnessing the energy found in chemicals or from sunlight. (credit: modification of work by Robert Bear, David Rintoul)

endergonic reaction of ATP phosphorylation is coupled to the exergonic reactions of catabolism. Similarly, the exergonic reaction of ATP dephosphorylation is coupled to the endergonic reaction of polypeptide formation, an example of anabolism.

Enzyme Structure and Function

A substance that helps speed up a chemical reaction is a catalyst. Catalysts are not used or changed during chemical reactions and, therefore, are reusable. Whereas inorganic molecules may serve as catalysts for a wide range of chemical reactions, proteins called enzymes serve as catalysts for biochemical reactions inside cells. Enzymes thus play an important role in controlling cellular metabolism.

An enzyme functions by lowering the activation energy of a chemical reaction inside the cell. Activation energy is the energy needed to form or break chemical bonds and convert reactants to products (Figure 8.5). Enzymes lower the activation energy by binding to the reactant molecules and holding them in such a way as to speed up the reaction. The chemical reactants to which an enzyme binds are called substrates, and the location within the enzyme where the substrate binds is called the enzyme’s active site. The characteristics of the amino acids near the active site create a very specific chemical environment within the active site that induces suitability to binding, albeit briefly, to a specific substrate (or substrates). Due to this jigsaw puzzle-like match between an enzyme and its substrates, enzymes are known for their specificity. In fact, as an enzyme binds to its substrate(s), the enzyme structure changes slightly to find the best fit between the transition state (a structural intermediate between the substrate and product) and the active site, just as a rubber glove molds to a hand inserted into it. This active-site modification in the presence of substrate, along with the simultaneous formation of the transition state, is called induced fit (Figure 8.6). Overall, there is a specifically matched enzyme for each substrate and, thus, for each chemical reaction; however, there is some flexibility as well. Some enzymes have the ability to act on several different structurally related substrates.
Figure 8.5 Enzymes lower the activation energy of a chemical reaction.
Figure 8.6 According to the induced-fit model, the active site of the enzyme undergoes conformational changes
upon binding with the substrate.

Enzymes are subject to influences by local environmental conditions such as pH, substrate concentration, and temperature. Although increasing the environmental temperature generally increases reaction rates, enzyme catalyzed or otherwise, increasing or decreasing the temperature outside of an optimal range can affect chemical bonds within the active site, making them less well suited to bind substrates. High temperatures will eventually cause enzymes, like other biological molecules, to denature, losing their three-dimensional structure and function. Enzymes are also suited to function best within a certain pH range, and, as with temperature, extreme environmental pH values (acidic or basic) can cause enzymes to denature. Active-site amino-acid side chains have their own acidic or basic properties that are optimal for catalysis and, therefore, are sensitive to changes in pH.

Another factor that influences enzyme activity is substrate concentration: Enzyme activity is increased at higher concentrations of substrate until it reaches a saturation point at which the enzyme can bind no additional substrate. Overall, enzymes are optimized to work best under the environmental conditions in which the organisms that produce them live. For example, while microbes that inhabit hot springs have enzymes that work best at high temperatures, human pathogens have enzymes that work best at 37°C. Similarly, while enzymes produced by most organisms work best at a neutral pH, microbes growing in acidic environments make enzymes optimized to low pH conditions, allowing for their growth at those conditions.

Many enzymes do not work optimally, or even at all, unless bound to other specific nonprotein helper molecules, either temporarily through ionic or hydrogen bonds or permanently through stronger covalent bonds. Binding to these molecules promotes optimal conformation and function for their respective enzymes. Two types of helper molecules are cofactors and coenzymes. Cofactors are inorganic ions such as iron (Fe 2+) and magnesium (Mg 2+) that help stabilize enzyme conformation and function. One example of an enzyme that requires a metal ion as a cofactor is the enzyme that builds DNA molecules, DNA polymerase, which requires a bound zinc ion (Zn 2+) to function. Coenzymes are organic helper molecules that are required for enzyme action. Like enzymes, they are not consumed and, hence, are reusable. The most common sources of coenzymes are dietary vitamins. Some vitamins are precursors to coenzymes and others act directly as coenzymes.

Some cofactors and coenzymes, like coenzyme A (CoA), often bind to the enzyme’s active site, aiding in the chemistry of the transition of a substrate to a product (Figure 8.7). In such cases, an enzyme lacking a necessary cofactor or coenzyme is called an apoenzyme and is inactive. Conversely, an enzyme with the necessary associated cofactor or coenzyme is called a holoenzyme and is active. NADH and ATP are also both examples of commonly used coenzymes that provide high-energy electrons or phosphate groups, respectively, which bind to enzymes, thereby activating them.
Figure 8.7 The binding of a coenzyme or cofactor to an apoenzyme is often required to form an active holoenzyme.

Enzyme Inhibitors

Enzymes can be regulated in ways that either promote or reduce their activity. There are many different kinds of molecules that inhibit or promote enzyme function, and various mechanisms exist for doing so (Figure 8.8). A competitive inhibitor is a molecule similar enough to a substrate that it can compete with the substrate for binding to the active site by simply blocking the substrate from binding. For a competitive inhibitor to be effective, the inhibitor concentration needs to be approximately equal to the substrate concentration. Sulfa drugs provide a good example of competitive competition. They are used to treat bacterial infections because they bind to the active site of an enzyme within the bacterial folic acid synthesis pathway. When present in a sufficient dose, a sulfa drug prevents folic acid synthesis, and bacteria are unable to grow because they cannot synthesize DNA, RNA, and proteins. Humans are unaffected because we obtain folic acid from our diets.

On the other hand, a noncompetitive (allosteric) inhibitor binds to the enzyme at an allosteric site, a location other than the active site, and still manages to block substrate binding to the active site by inducing a conformational change that reduces the affinity of the enzyme for its substrate (Figure 8.9). Because only one inhibitor molecule is needed per enzyme for effective inhibition, the concentration of inhibitors needed for noncompetitive inhibition is typically much lower than the substrate concentration.

In addition to allosteric inhibitors, there are allosteric activators that bind to locations on an enzyme away from the active site, inducing a conformational change that increases the affinity of the enzyme’s active site(s) for its substrate(s).

Allosteric control is an important mechanism of regulation of metabolic pathways involved in both catabolism and anabolism. In a most efficient and elegant way, cells have evolved also to use the products of their own metabolic reactions for feedback inhibition of enzyme activity. Feedback inhibition involves the use of a pathway product to regulate its own further production. The cell responds to the abundance of specific products by slowing production during anabolic or catabolic reactions (Figure 8.9).
Figure 8.8 Enzyme activity can be regulated by either competitive inhibitors, which bind to the active site, or
noncompetitive inhibitors, which bind to an allosteric site.
Figure 8.9 (a) Binding of an allosteric inhibitor reduces enzyme activity, but binding of an allosteric activator

increases enzyme activity. (b) Feedback inhibition, where the end product of the pathway serves as a noncompetitive inhibitor to an enzyme early in the pathway, is an important mechanism of allosteric regulation in cells. • Explain the difference between a competitive inhibitor and a noncompetitive inhibitor.

Of the 92 naturally occurring elements of the Earth crust, about 25 (i.e., B, C, Ca, Cl, Co, Cr, Cu, F, Fe, H, I, K, Mg, Mn, Mo, N, Na, O, P, S, Se, Si, Sn, V, and Zn) are essential for the cell. Of them, four (O, C, H, and N) comprise over 99% of the total weight of a cell, followed by P, S, Fe, and Ca. Elements are pure substances made of one kind of atom. Elements in the cell exist as ions (such as Na+ and Mg2+) and molecules, including inorganic compounds and organic compounds. Molecules are made of two or more atoms of the same (say, two oxygen atoms make a molecule of O2) or different (say, two hydrogen and one oxygen atoms make a molecule of H2O) kinds, attached by a covalent or ionic bond.

blocks.text: Biochemistry is the discipline that studies the chemistry of life, and its objective is to explain form and function based on chemical principles. Organic chemistry is the discipline devoted to the study of carbon-based chemistry, which is the foundation for the study of biomolecules and the discipline of biochemistry. Both biochemistry and organic chemistry are based on the concepts of general chemistry, some of which are presented in Appendix A. Elements in Living Cells The most abundant element in cells is hydrogen (H), followed by carbon (C), oxygen (O), nitrogen (N), phosphorous (P), and sulfur (S). We call these elements macronutrients, and they account for about 99% of the dry weight of cells. Some elements, such as sodium (Na), potassium (K), magnesium (Mg), zinc (Zn), iron (Fe), calcium (Ca), molybdenum (Mo), copper (Cu), cobalt (Co), manganese (Mn), or vanadium (Va), are required by some cells in very small amounts and are called micronutrients or trace elements. All of these elements are essential to the function of many biochemical reactions, and, therefore, are essential to life.

The four most abundant elements in living matter (C, N, O, and H) have low atomic numbers and are thus light elements capable of forming strong bonds with other atoms to produce molecules (Figure 7.2). Carbon forms four chemical bonds, whereas nitrogen forms three, oxygen forms two, and hydrogen forms one. When bonded together within molecules, oxygen, sulfur, and nitrogen often have one or more “lone pairs” of electrons that play important roles in determining many of the molecules’ physical and chemical properties (see Appendix A). These traits in combination permit the formation of a vast number of diverse molecular species necessary to form the structures and enable the functions of living organisms.

skeletons are held together by covalent bonds. They form the cells of an organism and perform the chemical reactions that facilitate life. All of these molecules, called biomolecules because they are part of living matter, contain carbon, which is the building block of life. Carbon is a very unique element in that it has four valence electrons in its outer orbitals and can form four single covalent bonds with up to four other atoms at the same time (see Appendix A). These atoms are usually oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulfur, phosphorous, and carbon itself; the simplest organic compound is methane, in which carbon binds only to hydrogen (Figure 7.3).

As a result of carbon’s unique combination of size and bonding properties, carbon atoms can bind together in large numbers, thus producing a chain or carbon skeleton. The carbon skeleton of organic molecules can be straight, branched, or ring shaped (cyclic). Organic molecules are built on chains of carbon atoms of varying lengths; most are typically very long, which allows for a huge number and variety of compounds. No other element has the ability to form so many different molecules of so many different sizes and shapes.
Figure 7.3 A carbon atom can bond with up to four other atoms. The simplest organic molecule is methane (CH 4 ),
depicted here.

Molecules with the same atomic makeup but different structural arrangement of atoms are called isomers. The concept of isomerism is very important in chemistry because the structure of a molecule is always directly related to its function. Slight changes in the structural arrangements of atoms in a molecule may lead to very different properties. Chemists represent molecules by their structural formula, which is a graphic representation of the molecular structure, showing how the atoms are arranged. Compounds that have identical molecular formulas but differ in the bonding sequence of the atoms are called structural isomers. The monosaccharides glucose, galactose, and fructose all have the same molecular formula, C6H 12O 6, but we can see from Figure 7.4 that the atoms are bonded together differently.
Figure 7.4 Glucose, galactose, and fructose have the same chemical formula (C 6 H 12 O6 ), but these structural
isomers differ in their physical and chemical properties.

Isomers that differ in the spatial arrangements of atoms are called stereoisomers; one unique type is enantiomers. The properties of enantiomers were originally discovered by Louis Pasteur in 1848 while using a microscope to analyze crystallized fermentation products of wine. Enantiomers are molecules that have the characteristic of chirality, in which their structures are nonsuperimposable mirror images of each other. Chirality is an important characteristic in many biologically important molecules, as illustrated by the examples of structural differences in the enantiomeric forms of the monosaccharide glucose or the amino acid alanine (Figure 7.5).

Many organisms are only able to use one enantiomeric form of certain types of molecules as nutrients and as building blocks to make structures within a cell. Some enantiomeric forms of amino acids have distinctly different tastes and smells when consumed as food. For example, L-aspartame, commonly called aspartame, tastes sweet, whereas D- aspartame is tasteless. Drug enantiomers can have very different pharmacologic affects. For example, the compound methorphan exists as two enantiomers, one of which acts as an antitussive (dextromethorphan, a cough suppressant), whereas the other acts as an analgesic (levomethorphan, a drug similar in effect to codeine).
Figure 7.5 Enantiomers are stereoisomers that exhibit chirality. Their chemical structures are nonsuperimposable

mirror images of each other. (a) D-glucose and L-glucose are monosaccharides that are enantiomers. (b) The enantiomers D-alanine and L-alanine are enantiomers found in bacterial cell walls and human cells, respectively. Enantiomers are also called optical isomers because they can rotate the plane of polarized light. Some of the crystals Pasteur observed from wine fermentation rotated light clockwise whereas others rotated the light counterclockwise. Today, we denote enantiomers that rotate polarized light clockwise (+) as d forms, and the mirror image of the same molecule that rotates polarized light counterclockwise (−) as the l form. The d and l labels are derived from the Latin words dexter (on the right) and laevus (on the left), respectively. These two different optical isomers often have very different biological properties and activities. Certain species of molds, yeast, and bacteria, such as Rhizopus, Yarrowia, and Lactobacillus spp., respectively, can only metabolize one type of optical isomer; the opposite isomer is not suitable as a source of nutrients. Another important reason to be aware of optical isomers is the therapeutic use of these types of chemicals for drug treatment, because some microorganisms can only be affected by one specific optical isomer.

Biologically Significant Functional Groups

In addition to containing carbon atoms, biomolecules also contain functional groups—groups of atoms within molecules that are categorized by their specific chemical composition and the chemical reactions they perform, regardless of the molecule in which the group is found. Some of the most common functional groups are listed in Figure 7.6. In the formulas, the symbol R stands for “residue” and represents the remainder of the molecule. R might symbolize just a single hydrogen atom or it may represent a group of many atoms. Notice that some functional groups are relatively simple, consisting of just one or two atoms, while some comprise two of these simpler functional groups. For example, a carbonyl group is a functional group composed of a carbon atom double bonded to an oxygen atom: C=O. It is present in several classes of organic compounds as part of larger functional groups such as ketones, aldehydes, carboxylic acids, and amides. In ketones, the carbonyl is present as an internal group, whereas in aldehydes it is a terminal group.

Figure 7.6 Macromolecules Carbon chains form the skeletons of most organic molecules. Functional groups combine with the chain to form biomolecules. Because these biomolecules are typically large, we call them macromolecules. Many biologically relevant macromolecules are formed by linking together a great number of identical, or very similar, smaller organic molecules. The smaller molecules act as building blocks and are called monomers, and the macromolecules that result from their linkage are called polymers. Cells and cell structures include four main groups of carbon-containing macromolecules: polysaccharides, proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids. The first three groups of molecules will be studied throughout this chapter. The biochemistry of nucleic acids will be discussed in Biochemistry of the Genome.

Of the many possible ways that monomers may be combined to yield polymers, one common approach encountered in the formation of biological macromolecules is dehydration synthesis. In this chemical reaction, monomer molecules bind end to end in a process that results in the formation of water molecules as a byproduct: H—monomer—OH + H—monomer—OH ⟶ H—monomer—monomer—OH + H 2 O

blocks.text: Ionic compounds are created by ionic bonds. An ionic bond forms between a positively charged ion (i.e., cation) and a negatively charged ion (i.e., anion). The table salt sodium chloride (NaCl) is an ionic compound formed by electrostatic attraction between Na+ and Cl- ions (Fig. 4.2).

Covalent compounds are formed by covalent bonds. A covalent bond is formed when two different atoms share a pair of electrons (Fig. 4.2). Two atoms may share one, two, three, four, or even five pairs of electrons, creating 1, 2, 3,4 and 5 covalent bonds between them. Molecular nitrogen (N2) molecules are formed when two N atoms share three pairs of electrons.
Fig. 4.2. Chemical bonds. A. Ionic bonds are formed between an anion and a cation. B. Covalent bonds are formed

when two atoms share pairs of electrons. C. Hydrogen bonds are formed between the d+ and d- induction of two polar covalent compounds through a hydrogen atom. The van der Waals force acts between two atoms with opposite induced dipoles. Images- A, B, and C: Chemistrtylearner.com. D- IScollege.ac.

Covalent compounds can be nonpolar if the shared electron pairs are equally shared by the two atoms. If one of the two partners attracts the shared election pair more than the other, creating a partial negative charge ( d-) around itself. The other partner atom creates a partial positive charge (d+) around itself. Such a situation frequently occurs if an oxygen or nitrogen atom forms a covalent bond with a hydrogen atom. The electrostatic attraction between (d-) and (d+) regions of such molecules creates a hydrogen bond (Fig. 4.2).

The electrons of any atom may occasionally shift to one side of the atom, creating a negative induction on that side and a positive induction on the other side. Two atoms with such inductions may develop a weak and temporary attractive force known as the van der Waals force (Fig. 4.2), if the two atoms are in the proper orientation and within a distance of 0.3-0.6 nanometers (the force won't develop if the two atoms are closer or further apart). The amount of heat energy needed to break a bond is the bond energy. The average bond energy for various bonds is shown in Table 4.1. Covalent bonds and some ionic bonds are considered strong bonds, and such bonds create molecules. Some ionic bonds, all hydrogen bonds, and van der Waals forces are weak bonds/interactions; they do not create molecules.

Inorganic compounds are molecules lacking a carbon (C) atom. Water (H2O) is the most abundant inorganic molecule of the cell (Table 4.2). Other than water, inorganic molecules exist as ions or are bound to organic molecules. The common inorganic molecules of the cell include CO2 (as bicarbonate ion HCO3-), NaCl (as Na+ and Cl- ions), Ca3(PO4)2 (as Ca2+ and PO43- ions), NH4OH (as NH4+ and OH- ions), KI (as K+ and I- ions) and FeSO4 (as Fe2+ and SO42- ions). weight. Modified from Watson JD. Molecular Biology of Genes, 2nd Ed., Saunders, Philadelphia (1972). Water 70.0% Proteins 15.0% Amino acid metabolites 0.8% RNA 6.0% DNA 1.0% Nucleotide metabolites 0.8% Polysaccharide and sugar metabolites 3.0% Lipids and lipid metabolites 2.0% Minerals and trace elements 1.0% Others 0.4% Since water forms the bulk volume of the cell, the properties of water influence the physiology of the cell very immensely. Water is a polar covalent compound; its O atom has a partial negative charge (d-) and the two hydrogen atoms have partial positive charge ( d+). It allows one water molecule to form four hydrogen bonds with four other water molecules (Fig. 4.3). Ionic inorganic compounds readily interact with water and dissociate. For example, NaCl dissolves in water and dissociates to Na+ and Cl- ions.

Molecules that readily dissolve in water are hydrophilic (water-loving). The solubility of inorganic and polar organic compounds allows the cell to readily absorb those nutrients. However, nonpolar covalent compounds, such as lipids, are hydrophobic (water-fearing) and cannot interact with water. Hydrophobic molecules, like any other molecules, can interact with one another through van der Waals forces. Water molecules exclude hydrophobic molecules, allowing water molecules to interact with each other and causing hydrophobic molecules to clump together (Fig. 4.3). This phenomenon, called hydrophobic interactions, enables the formation of lipid membranes.
Fig. 4.3. Hydrogen bond formation and hydrophobic interactions. A. Water is polar because it has its oxygen atom

with a partial positive charge and hydrogen atoms with a partial negative charge. The bond between these partially negative and positive charges is a hydrogen bond. Image- USGS. B. Hydrophobic interactions. Hydrophobic molecules (the hexagons) can interact with each other but not with water molecules (winged balls). Water molecules cause hydrophobic molecules to aggregate, allowing water molecules to interact with each other. Image-Hawaii.edu. Water also poses some changes to the cell. Since water molecules are small and uncharged, they can pass through the plasma membrane very easily. It poses the cell with the problem of osmosis and the osmotic pressure (the pressure on the plasma membrane due to the movement of water molecules). The cytoplasm contains bout 1% dissolved salts. If a cell is placed in pure water (containing ~0% salt), water from outside the cell enters the cytoplasm, causing the cell to burst, unless the cell has a strong cell wall (as in algae and bacteria), or the cell pumps water out of the cell. In contrast, if a cell is placed in brine or seawater (3.5% salt), cytoplasmic water moves out, causing the cytoplasm to shrink, leading to cell death. Microbiologists often use osmotic pressure to control microbial growth. When molecules dissociate in water, they create ions, including some highly reactive and toxic ions. For example, acidic compounds dissolve and dissociate in water, releasing protons (H+), while basic or alkaline compounds dissolve and dissociate in water, releasing hydroxide (OH-) ions. Protons (H+) react with water to create hydronium ions (H3O+). The concentration of H3O+ in aqueous solutions is expressed as the potential of hydrogen (pH), calculated using the formula -log [H+ concentration in moles per liter]. In pure water, 1 in 10,000,000 (i.e., 107) water molecules dissociate into H+ and OH- ions. Thus, the concentration of H+ (or H3O+) in pure water is 1×10-7 mole/liter, giving a pH of 7, which is considered the neutral pH. Since pH is calculated in the negative log, the lower the pH, the higher the H+ concentration in a solution.

If acidic molecules dissolve in water and release more H+, the pH drops below 7 (i.e., the solution turns acidic). Likewise, if basic substances dissolve in water and release OH- ions, the OH- ions react with H+ and produce water (H+ + OH- à H2O). The removal of protons increases the pH above 7 (i.e., making it a basic solution). The pH range of an aqueous solution is 0-14. Since H+ and OH- ions are highly reactive (they can react with proteins and nucleic acids of the cell and damage them), the cell tolerates a very narrow pH range. The cell creates a buffered solution by mixing acids and bases in the cytoplasm, maintaining a homeostatic pH of 7.4. Microbiologists manipulate pH to control microbial growth. However, some microbes have a special ability to thrive at extreme acidic pH of 2 or extreme basic pH of 12.

slides.title: Organic compounds of the cell: Lipids

blocks.text: Organic compounds contain one or more C atoms. Organic compounds can be created by only C and H atoms. Such compounds are called hydrocarbons. Petroleum (propane, octane, etc.) are hydrocarbons. Some atoms or groups of atoms, known as functional groups, may replace one or more H atoms in a hydrocarbon, creating a wide range of organic compounds.

Common functional groups include chlorine (Cl), aldehyde (CHO), hydroxyl (-OH), carbonyl (C=O), carboxylic (COOH), amine (NH2), phosphate (PO4), and sulfhydryl (SH). These functional groups can create diverse organic molecules (Fig. 4.4) by replacing H atoms of the hydrocarbon methane (CH4). Different functional groups give organic compounds radically different chemical and physical properties. For example, methane is a toxic, flammable gas; methanol and chloroform are toxic liquids; acetaldehyde is a nontoxic liquid and a potential carcinogen; and acetic acid is a consumable liquid present in many food products (Fig. 4.4).
Fig. 4.4. Importance of the functional groups. Showing various compounds generated from a molecule of methane

by substituting certain H atoms with various functional groups. The names of the compounds are indicated. The functional groups in each of the compounds that substituted the H atoms of methane are circled. The organic molecules of the cell are extremely diverse. However, they can be grouped into small or precursor molecules and complex or large macromolecules. Many macromolecules are polymers, composed of many units of one or more types of precursor molecules. Precursor molecules are either synthesized in the cell or imported from the surroundings and used as is. Macromolecules are synthesized inside the cell. If imported, the cell generally breaks the macromolecules and uses the resulting precursor molecules. The precursor molecules can be divided into four major groups: lipids, simple sugars, organic acids, and nucleotides.
Lipids
Lipids are water-insoluble organic molecules that can be extracted by nonpolar solvents such as acetone. Some of the important simple lipids of the cell are the following.
Hydrocarbons

Hydrocarbons have only C and H atoms, and an all-carbon skeleton (Fig. 4.5). Hydrocarbons can be linear, branched, cyclic, or a mixture thereof. Archaea, some bacterial plant cells contain isoprenoids, a type of branched-chain hydrocarbons.
Fatty acids

A fatty acid (Fig. 4.5) is an unbranched hydrocarbon with a -COOH group. Vegetable oils, tallow, and lard are mostly fatty acids (i.e., oleic acid, palmitic acid, and stearic acid). Fatty acids found in the cell have 12-18 carbon atoms. Glycerolipids, phospholipids, sphingolipids, and glycolipids Glycerolipids are composed of a molecule of glycerol (a three-carbon alcohol) and 1-3 fatty acids or isoprenoid chains (Fig. 4.5). One, two, or three fatty acid molecules linked to a glycerol molecule produce mono-, di-, or triglycerides. A mono- or diglyceride with a -PO4 group attached to the carbon position 1 (for archaea) or 3 (all other cell types) of the glycerol molecules is called a phospholipid (Fig. 4.4). Sphingolipids are made of one sphingosine or a related molecule and one fatty acid chain (Fig 4.5). Glycolipids are glycerolipids or sphingolipids to which a short chain of sugars (polysaccharides) is attached.

While hydrocarbons and fatty acids are highly hydrophobic, glycerolipids, phospholipids, sphingolipids, and glycolipids are amphiphilic (or amphipathic), having the hydrophobic fatty acid tail and a hydrophobic head group made of glycerol, phosphate group, sugar, and additional molecules such as ethanolamine. Amphipathic lipids are exclusively used to form cellular membranes.
Fig. 4.5. Some lipids. A hydrocarbon has only made of C and H atoms. Shown is, octane, a linear hydrocarbon

containing 8 C atoms. A fatty acid is linear hydrocarbon with one -COOH group. A glycerol molecule has tree carbon atoms (the middle C atom is not shown). A diglyceride has two fatty acids attached to the C atoms 2 and 3 attached to tow fatty acids. A phosphoglycerolipid has one or two fatty acids and a PO4 group attached to the glycerol molecule. Cholesterol is a sterol found in the membrane of animal cells.

Other important lipids present in the cell include ubiquinone (i.e., coenzyme Q10), retinoic acid, vitamins A, E, and K, arachidonic acid, prostaglandins, and thromboxanes. Some cells produce long-chain carboxylic acids known as waxes. Mycolic acid of mycobacteria are wax-like fatty acids. Lipids can be attached to polysaccharides to produce lipopolysaccharides (see Chapter 2), or to proteins to produce lipoproteins.
Steroids and sterols

Steroids (Fig. 4.5) are lipids containing four fused carbon rings. A sterol is a steroid with one or more -OH groups. Cholesterol, found in animal cells, and ergosterol, found in fungi, are sterols. Some hormones (such as testosterone, estrogen, cortisol, and aldosterone) and vitamin D are structurally similar to cholesterol. Sterols of plant cells are phytosterols. Prokaryotes lack sterols, but some bacteria have related chemical compounds such as hopanoids. Simple sugars Simple sugars are carbohydrates, made of C, H, and O, where the ratio of H and O is 2:1. Simple sugars (also called monosaccharides) contain an all-carbon skeleton, several –OH groups, and one - CHO or a –C=O group. The carbon skeleton of monosaccharides can be linear or partially cyclic (Fig. 4.6). The number of carbons in the skeleton could be 3, 4, 5, 6, or 7, and the corresponding sugars are named triose, tetrose, pentose, hexose, and heptose, respectively. Pentoses such as ribose and deoxyribose are the major components of nucleotides. Hexoses such as glucose and fructose are the major nutritional and structural molecules of the cell.

Two or more organic compounds could have the same molecular formula but different structures. Such molecules are called isomers. Simple sugar can be dextral (D isoform) or levorotary (L isoform) because of the arrangement of an OH group. Cells usually use the D isoform of sugars.

Two simple sugars connected by a covalent bond (called a glycosidic bond) create a disaccharide. Table sugar (sucrose) is made of one glucose and one fructose, while milk sugar (lactose) is made of one glucose and one galactose unit (Fig. 4.6). Glucose, fructose, and galactose are hexose sugars.
Fig. 4.6. Some common simple sugars. Shown are the monosaccharides glyceraldehyde, D-ribose, D-glucose, N-
acetyl glucosamine, and the disaccharide lactose. Lactose is made of a D-glucose linked by a β-glycosidic bond to a D-galactose.
Carboxylic acids

A simple carboxylic acid has the formula R-COOH. Some of the carboxylic acids in the cell are acetic acid, pyruvic acid, citric acid, propionic acid, and succinic acid (Fig. 4.7). To manage the pH of the cells, these acids are converted into conjugate bases (acetate, pyruvate, citrate, and propionate). Carboxylic acids are used in the synthesis of ATP and other molecules, including fatty acids and amino acids.
Fig. 4.7. Some common carboxylic acids. Shown are acetic acid, pyruvic acid, propionic acid, and citric acid.
Amino acids

An amino acid is a carboxylic acid with an amine group. The alpha amino acids have an H atom, a –COOH group, a -NH2 group, and a radical (R) group directly attached to a central carbon atom (called the α-carbon). The NH2 and COOH groups attached to the alpha C atoms are called the primary amino and primary carboxyl groups, to distinguish them from other such groups found in the R group. A radical group is a larger functional group (Fig. 4.8). The cell uses 22 alpha amino acids for protein synthesis; of them, 20 are universally present in proteins (Fig. 4.8). Since all alpha amino acids are identical except the R group, the R group determines the chemical properties of the amino acids.
Fig. 4.8. The 20 common alpha amino acids the cell uses for protein synthesis. The R groups are shaded. The
amino acids are grouped into nonpolar, polar, positively charged, and negatively charged, based on the chemical properties of their R groups. (CC)- Bio Ninja.
Nucleotides

Nucleotides are made of a pentose sugar, a nitrogenous base, and 1-3 phosphate groups. The nitrogenous bases are so named because certain nitrogen atoms of the compounds behave like a weak base such as ammonia (NH3). Two types of nitrogenous bases, pyrimidines (i.e., thymine, cytosine, and uracil) and purines (i.e., adenine and guanine) are used in synthesizing nucleotides (Fig 4.9).
Fig. 4.9. The components of nucleotides. A. Ribose and deoxyribose sugars. B. The two purine bases (adenine and

guanine) and the three pyrimidine bases (cytosine, uracil, and thymine). C. Examples of nucleosides (shown are adenosine and 2’deoxythymidine). D. Example of a nucleotide. Shown is a deoxyadenosine triphosphate (dATP). The three phosphate groups of dATP (or ATP) are named as the a, b and g phosphates.

Pentose sugars found in nucleotides are ribose or deoxyribose. Ribose and deoxyribose are identical except in the carbon position 2’, where the ribose sugar has the H-C-OH configuration, but the deoxyribose sugar has the H-C-H configuration (Fig. 4.9).

When a nitrogenous base is attached to the carbon atom at position 1’ of the pentose sugar, the resulting compound is a nucleoside (Fig.4.7). The eight possible nucleosides are adenosine (A), guanosine (G), uridine (U), cytidine (C), deoxyadenosine (dA), deoxyguanosine (dG), deoxythymidine (dC), and deoxycytidine (dT) (Fig. 4.9). When phosphate groups are attached to a nucleoside, the resulting compound is a nucleotide (. 4.9). One, two, or three phosphate groups attached to a nucleoside produce a nucleoside monophosphate (or NMPs), nucleoside diphosphate (or NDPs), and nucleoside triphosphate (or NTPs), respectively. The four nucleotides used in synthesizing RNA are the ribonucleotides ATP, CTP, GTP, and UTP, and the four nucleotides used in synthesizing DNA are the deoxyribonucleotides dATP, dCTP, dGTP and dTTP.
Coenzymes

Coenzymes are diverse groups of organic molecules needed for some enzyme-catalyzed reactions. Some of the most important coenzymes are ATP, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP+), flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), co-enzyme A (Co-A), and tetrahydrofolate (Fig. 4.10).
Fig. 4.10. Some coenzymes. Shown are NAD+, FAD, Co-A, and tetrahydrofolate. If a phosphate group replaces the
H atom indicated by the red arrow of NAD+; NAD+ turns to NADP+. If two H atoms are attached to the two N atoms (indicated by the blue arrows) of FAD, FAD turn to FADH2.

blocks.text: The most abundant biomolecules on earth are carbohydrates. From a chemical viewpoint, carbohydrates are primarily a combination of carbon and water, and many of them have the empirical formula (CH 2O) n, where n is the number of repeated units. This view represents these molecules simply as “hydrated” carbon atom chains in which water molecules attach to each carbon atom, leading to the term “carbohydrates.” Although all carbohydrates contain carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, there are some that also contain nitrogen, phosphorus, and/or sulfur. Carbohydrates have myriad different functions. They are abundant in terrestrial ecosystems, many forms of which we use as food sources. These molecules are also vital parts of macromolecular structures that store and transmit genetic information (i.e., DNA and RNA). They are the basis of biological polymers that impart strength to various structural components of organisms (e.g., cellulose and chitin), and they are the primary source of energy storage in the form of starch and glycogen.
Monosaccharides: The Sweet Ones

In biochemistry, carbohydrates are often called saccharides, from the Greek sakcharon, meaning sugar, although not all the saccharides are sweet. The simplest carbohydrates are called monosaccharides, or simple sugars. They are the building blocks (monomers) for the synthesis of polymers or complex carbohydrates, as will be discussed further in this section. Monosaccharides are classified based on the number of carbons in the molecule. General categories are identified using a prefix that indicates the number of carbons and the suffix –ose, which indicates a saccharide; for example, triose (three carbons), tetrose (four carbons), pentose (five carbons), and hexose (six carbons) (Figure 7.8). The hexose D-glucose is the most abundant monosaccharide in nature. Other very common and abundant hexose monosaccharides are galactose, used to make the disaccharide milk sugar lactose, and the fruit sugar fructose.
Figure 7.8 Monosaccharides are classified based on the position of the carbonyl group and the number of carbons
in the backbone.

Monosaccharides of four or more carbon atoms are typically more stable when they adopt cyclic, or ring, structures. These ring structures result from a chemical reaction between functional groups on opposite ends of the sugar’s flexible carbon chain, namely the carbonyl group and a relatively distant hydroxyl group. Glucose, for example, forms a six-membered ring (Figure 7.9).
Figure 7.9 (a) A linear monosaccharide (glucose in this case) forms a cyclic structure. (b) This illustration shows a
more realistic depiction of the cyclic monosaccharide structure. Note in these cyclic structural diagrams, the carbon atoms composing the ring are not explicitly shown.
• Why do monosaccharides form ring structures?
Disaccharides

Two monosaccharide molecules may chemically bond to form a disaccharide. The name given to the covalent bond between the two monosaccharides is a glycosidic bond. Glycosidic bonds form between hydroxyl groups of the two saccharide molecules, an example of the dehydration synthesis described in the previous section of this chapter: monosaccharide—OH + HO—monosaccharide ⟶ monosaccharide—O—monosaccharide ⎤ ⎦ ⎥ ⎥ ⎥ ⎥ ⎥ ⎥ ⎥ ⎥ ⎥ ⎥ ⎥ ⎥ ⎥ ⎥ disaccharide Common disaccharides are the grain sugar maltose, made of two glucose molecules; the milk sugar lactose, made of a galactose and a glucose molecule; and the table sugar sucrose, made of a glucose and a fructose molecule (Figure 7.10).
Figure 7.10 Common disaccharides include maltose, lactose, and sucrose.
Polysaccharides

Polysaccharides, also called glycans, are large polymers composed of hundreds of monosaccharide monomers. Unlike mono- and disaccharides, polysaccharides are not sweet and, in general, they are not soluble in water. Like disaccharides, the monomeric units of polysaccharides are linked together by glycosidic bonds.

Polysaccharides are very diverse in their structure. Three of the most biologically important polysaccharides—starch, glycogen, and cellulose—are all composed of repetitive glucose units, although they differ in their structure (Figure 7.11). Cellulose consists of a linear chain of glucose molecules and is a common structural component of cell walls in plants and other organisms. Glycogen and starch are branched polymers; glycogen is the primary energy-storage molecule in animals and bacteria, whereas plants primarily store energy in starch. The orientation of the glycosidic linkages in these three polymers is different as well and, as a consequence, linear and branched macromolecules have different properties.

Modified glucose molecules can be fundamental components of other structural polysaccharides. Examples of these types of structural polysaccharides are N-acetyl glucosamine (NAG) and N-acetyl muramic acid (NAM) found in bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan. Polymers of NAG form chitin, which is found in fungal cell walls and in the exoskeleton of insects.
Figure 7.11 Starch, glycogen, and cellulose are three of the most important polysaccharides. In the top row,

hexagons represent individual glucose molecules. Micrographs (bottom row) show wheat starch granules stained with iodine (left), glycogen granules (G) inside the cell of a cyanobacterium (middle), and bacterial cellulose fibers (right). (credit “iodine granules”: modification of work by Kiselov Yuri; credit “glycogen granules”: modification of work by Stöckel J, Elvitigala TR, Liberton M, Pakrasi HB; credit “cellulose”: modification of work by American Society for Microbiology) • What are the most biologically important polysaccharides and why are they important?
Macromolecules are large organic molecules, including some lipids (described in the previous section), and biopolymers such as polysaccharides, proteins, and nucleic acids.
Polysaccharides

A polysaccharide molecule contains many units of monosaccharides, and the molecules could be linear or highly branched. Large polysaccharides are insoluble in water and serve as stored energy sources or structural components, such as the cell wall. There are many types of polysaccharides in nature (Fig. 4 .11).
Fig. 4.11. Some common polysaccharides found in the cell. A. Hyaluronic acid, a major polysaccharide of skin and

tissue matrices, is made of D-glucuronic acid and N-acetyl glucosamine. B. Cellulose, the major polymer of the plant cell wall, is made of D-glucose. C. Chitin, a polymer present in fungi and arthropods, is made of N-acetyl glucosamine. D. Murein of the bacterial cell wall is made of N-acetyl glucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM). Glycogen is the major food storage polysaccharide of animal and fungal cells. Animals also contain heparan sulfate, heparin, hyaluronates, and some other polysaccharides for structural purposes. Fungal cell walls and some insects contain a type of polysaccharide called chitin. Plant cells contain various types of polysaccharides, including cellulose for structure and starches such as amylose and amylopectin as stored nutrients. The basic chemical structures of some of the polysaccharides are shown in Fig. 4.11.
Nucleic acids

Nucleic acids are linear or circular (but never branched) polymers of nucleotides (Fig. 4.12). The two types of nucleic acids are ribonucleic acids (RNA, made of AMP, GMP, CMP, and UMP) and deoxyribonucleic acids (DNA, made of dAMP, dGMP, dCMP, and dTMP). DNA and RNA are called nucleic acids because they were originally isolated from the nucleus of eukaryotic cells and contain phosphate groups (i.e., PO4), which are remnants of phosphoric acid (H3PO4).
Fig. 4.12. Single- and double-stranded nucleic acids. A. A linear single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) molecule

containing 4 nucleotides. By convention, the nucleotide sequence of the molecule reads 5’CAUG3’. B. A double- stranded DNA (dsDNA) molecule made of two ssDNA molecules 5’AGAG3’ and 5’CTCT3’ with A and T, and C and G on the opposite strands base-paired (forming hydrogen bonds). The arrows show the orientation of the two strands. The ribose sugar at the 5’ end has three PO4 groups, and the one at the 3’ end has an open -OH group. A nucleic acid has a sugar-phosphate backbone, which acts like a vine to which the nitrogenous bases appear as leaves attached to the carbon position 1’ of each of the pentose sugar (Fig. 4.12). The terminal nucleotide with its ribose attached to three phosphate groups is the 5’ end of a nucleic acid molecule. The other end, which has a free OH group at the third carbon atom of the ribose, is the 3’ end of a nucleic acid molecule. By convention, the nucleotide sequence of a nucleic acid molecule is written from the 5’ end towards the 3’ end (say, 5’CGATTCGG3’). All linear DNA or RNA molecules have 5’ and 3' ends, but circular nucleic acid molecules do not have an end.
Single- and double-stranded nucleic acids

A single molecule of nucleic acid not interacting with another molecule of nucleic acid is a single-stranded (or ss) nucleic acid molecule. Two ss-nucleic acid molecules may form a double-stranded (ds) nucleic acid molecule if they are complementary (have matching nucleotides) and antiparallel (paired in opposite length-wise orientation, Fig. 4.12). The A and T or U, and G and C bases of the opposite strands form hydrogen bonds (base-pairs), which help the two strands to stay paired. A single long ssRNA or ssDNA molecule can fold and form local double-stranded regions (Fog 4.13).

A nucleic acid molecule may contain a few to a few million nucleotides. The size of ssDNA or ssRNA is expressed in bases or nucleotides. For example, a tRNA molecule is 100 bases (or 100 b). The size of dsRNA or dsDNA is counted in base pairs (bp). The dsDNA genome of the human papillomavirus is 8,000 bp. A thousand, a million, and a billion base pairs (bp of DNA are expressed as kilobase pairs (kbp), megabase pairs (mbp), and giga base pairs (gbp), respectively. The size of the human genome 3.2 gbp.

The chromosomes of the cell are made of dsDNA, which has a specific structure known as the B-form DNA (Fig. 4.13). In B-form DNA, the two ssDNA strands stay 2 nanometers apart, and they form a right-handed helical structure, with 10.5 bp of DNA making one full turn of the helix. The A and T bases form two hydrogen bonds, and the G and C bases form three hydrogen bonds. The consecutive base pairs stay 0.34 nanometers away. Thus, the length of a chromosome can be measured by multiplying its size by 0.34 nm. The size of the human Y chromosome (size 60,0000,000 bp), its length is 60,0000,000 bp x 0.34 nanometers per bp, = 20,400,000 nm (i.e., 2.04 cm or 0.8 inches).
Fig. 4.13. Structures of the dsDNA and dsRNA. A. DNA double helix. The sugar-phosphate backbones of the two

anti-parallel ssDNA molecules (indicated as blue ribbons) stay at the margin (2 nm apart), and the base-pairs (shown as the steps of a ladder) stay in the core of the right-handed double helix. Each complete turn of the right-handed helix contains 10.5 base pairs of DNA. Image-NIH. B. Structure of a folded ssRNA molecule showing double-stranded stems and single-stranded loops. The stems are formed due to the hydrogen bonds formed between A and U and G and C base pairs.
Proteins

Proteins are linear polymers of alpha amino acids. Two amino acids form a dipeptide when the primary –COOH group of an amino acid reacts with the primary –NH2 group of another amino acid. The reaction releases a molecule of water (Fig. 4.14). The resulting N-C covalent bond is a peptide bond, and the compound is a dipeptide molecule.
Fig. 4.14. The primary and secondary structures of polypeptides. A. Synthesis of a dipeptide from two amino

acids. B. The primary structure of a polypeptide showing the N and the C termini. C. An α-helix is formed because of hydrogen bond formation. D. A β-sheet is formed due to the formation of hydrogen bonds. Image- Wikipedia. Many amino acids linked by peptide bonds create a polypeptide. A polypeptide having 75 or more amino acids is called a protein. The primary –NH2 group of the first amino acid and the primary - COOH group of the last amino acid of a polypeptide chain stay open, forming the amino (NH2 or N) and carboxyl (COOH) termini of the protein. The amino acid sequence of a protein is the primary structure of a protein. The amino acid sequence, by convention is written starting from N-terminus. For example, the amino acid sequence of the peptide hormone oxytocin is N-Cys- Tyr-Ile-Gln-Asn-Cys-Pro-Leu-Glu-C.

In aqueous solution, the N atom of the primary –NH2 group of one amino acid and the O atom of the primary –COOH group of another nearby amino acid of a polypeptide may form hydrogen bonds. As a result, certain areas of the polypeptide chain fold to form a helical structure called a helix, and/or a belt-like structure called b -sheets (Fig. 4.15), which are the secondary structures of a protein.

The functional groups of the R groups of amino acids of a protein also interact with each other via weak bonds, including hydrogen bonds and ionic bonds. The –SH group of the R group of two cysteine residues may form a disulfide (S-S) bond (which is a covalent bond). One of the major reasons for folding is to hide the hydrophobic amino acids in the core of a protein while exposing the hydrophilic amino acids on the protein's outer surface, where they are exposed to water/cytoplasm of the cell.

The above interactions give the polypeptide chain its three-dimensional tertiary structure (Fig. 4.15). Two or more identical or nonidentical polypeptide chains often fold together to form a three-dimensional quaternary structure (Fig. 4.15).
Fig. 4.15. The tertiary and quaternary structures of proteins. A. Various weak and strong bonds formed between

the R groups. B. The tertiary structure of a polypeptide chain with the hydrophilic amino acids on the outer margin (green) and the hydrophobic amino acids in the core (pink). C. quaternary structure of two polypeptides folded together. D. The tertiary structure of the enzyme chymotrypsin (an enzyme made of a single polypeptide chain). E. The quaternary structure of hemoglobin (made of four polypeptide chains). Images D and E-Wikipedia. In biology, structure is function. Although D-glucose and L-glucose are made of the same atoms and have the same molecular weight, they behave differently because of the slight differences in their structures. The same is true for nucleic acids and proteins. Mutations in DNA and RNA may prevent the formation of proper structures. Since the structures of these macromolecules are mostly determined by weak bonds (hydrophobic interaction, hydrogen bonds, and weak ionic bonds), which may break with slight changes in temperature and pH, or by chemical agents that interfere with weak bond formation, microbial growth can be controlled by manipulating temperature and pH and by applying various chemical agents.

sections.heading: Why and how chemical reactions occur in the cell

blocks.text: Whether a chemical reaction will take place can be predicted by the second law of thermodynamics, which states that the total entropy (disorder) of the system increases over time. Since disorder is caused by the movement of molecules and heat causes molecules to move, a chemical reaction may not occur unless some heat energy is allowed dissipate (get lost).

Chemical compounds formed by strong bonds are low-energy compounds, and those formed with some unstable covalent bonds are high-energy compounds. The chemical reaction A-B + C-D à A-C + B-D (where A-B and C-D are reactants, and A-C and B-D are products), does not take place if the reactants are low-energy molecules and the products are high-energy molecules, unless some heat energy is infused in the system.

However, if the reactants are high-energy and the products are low-energy, chemical reactions may proceed spontaneously to completion, because the heat energy of the high-energy compound will dissipate. Heat energy is measured in kilocalories (kcal), where 1 kcal is the heat required to raise the temperature of 1 liter of water by 1 degree Celsius. Note the following chemical reactions 6CO2 + 6H2O à C6H12O6 +6O2, ΔG= +686 kcal/mole --- --- (i) C6H12O6 +6O2 à 6CO2 + 6H2O, ΔG= -686 kcal/mole --- --- --- (ii) Here, ΔG is the difference in energy between the reactants and products. Reaction (i), the overall reaction of photosynthesis, is endergonic. It has a ΔG= +686 kcal/mole (the product has more energy than the reactants). This reaction would not take place unless 686 kcal/mole were added to the system.

Reaction II (i.e., caramelizing or oxidizing glucose) is an exergonic reaction; its ΔG= -686 kcal/mole indicates that the reactants have more energy than the products. This reaction would readily proceed, releasing 686 kcal/mol (Fig. 4.16).
Fig. 4.16. The energy diagram of the oxidation of glucose. Note that even though the ΔG for the chemical reaction

is negative, the reaction would not take place unless the required activation energy (ΔG‡) is infused into the system. The synthesis of glucose from CO2 and H2O (the reverse reaction) requires a much higher activation energy. However, if one places some glucose on a pan, it will not caramelize, even though 20% of the air molecules are oxygen, unless one heats the pan to 146 °C. The heat is necessary for the reactants to move and collide before the chemical reaction can take place.

The amount of energy required to initiate a chemical reaction, even an exergonic one, is the activation energy, which enables reactant molecules to move and collide to react. The amount of activation energy needed to initiate an endergonic reaction is much higher compared to that for an exergonic reaction.

Chloroplasts conduct reaction (i), and all cells conduct reaction (ii) all the time, but the activation energy listed above to initiate the reactions would burn or evaporate the cells instantly. Then how do the cells conduct those chemical reactions?

The cells use two mechanisms to conduct chemical reactions: they use catalysts and break the overall reaction into many small steps, so that the energy infused or released does not exceed the physiological norm (i.e., about 37 °C). Catalysts are chemical agents that participate in chemical reactions and help reduce the activation energy required, but they are not consumed in the reaction. Consider the following reactions: A + B à AB DG is very high A +E à A-E DG is low AE + B à A-B + E DG is low The catalysts of the cell are enzymes. Enzymes are made of proteins, RNAs, or RNA-protein complexes. The enzymes have a 3-D structure with substrate-binding pockets and a reaction center (active site). The reactants bind to the enzyme with high affinity. The enzyme stresses the reactants and orients them for the reaction to take place. The product does not bind the enzyme, so it dissociates, leaving the enzyme to catalyze the next reaction (Fig. 4.17).
Fig. 4.17. An enzyme-catalyzed reaction: Glucose +ATP + enzyme à glucose-PO4 + ADP + enzyme. A. The

enzyme glucokinase and its substrates ATP and glucose. B. The enzyme binds its substrates in its substrate-binding pocket close to the active site of the enzyme. C. The enzyme temporarily changes its structure to bring the substrates close together and applies strain and stress to them. D. The products of the chemical reaction (i.e., glucose phosphate and ADP) are generated as a result. E. The enzyme regains its normal structure. The products cannot bind the enzyme's binding pocket, so they move away from the enzyme. The enzyme is now ready to catalyze another round of the chemical reaction.

An enzyme usually uses one or a few substrates and produces one or a few products. An enzyme may catalyze millions of a particular chemical reaction in a second. This allows cells to respond to environmental changes quickly and smoothly. Since one enzyme may only produce one product, several enzymes are needed to synthesize a complex molecule from simple precursors (Fig. 4.18). A group of enzyme-catalyzed reactions leading to the synthesis or breakdown of a metabolite is a metabolic pathway. The cell has many interconnected metabolic pathways. If one of the key enzymes in a metabolic pathway is mutated or inactivated by a drug or toxin, the entire pathway may be disrupted, causing cell death.
Fig. 4.18. The metabolic pathways. Three interconnected metabolic pathways (A-B-C-D, C-M-N-O-P, and N-W-X-

Y-Z) are shown. Each of the reactions (indicated by an arrow) is dependent on an enzyme (shown by the lower-case letters). Thus, the enzyme b catalyzes the synthesis of product C using substrate B. If the gene for the enzyme b is mutated, all three metabolic pathways may collapse. Also, if the enzyme b can be controlled, all the three metabolic pathways can be indirectly controlled.

Since enzymes catalyze chemical reactions so quickly, the cell regulates them in many ways to avoid chaos. Microbiologists may control microbial growth by manipulating microbial enzymes. Enzymes can be deactivated by altering temperature, pH, or by chemical agents that bind and inhibit them.

slides.title: High energy vs. low energy compounds

blocks.text: The cell has many high-energy compounds, including ATP, CTP, GTP, UTP, and creatine phosphate. However, the cell prefers ATP and synthesizes it to create other high-energy molecules. The cell also uses ATP to do work (work is moving an atom from one location to another). ATP is synthesized by the following chemical reaction ADP + PO4 à ATP, ΔG=+7.3 kcal/mol Since the reaction is endergonic, the cell uses other forms of energy to synthesize ATP. Photosynthetic bacteria and chloroplasts use light energy; other cells use the bond energy of other high-energy molecules, known as food molecules, to synthesize ATP. There are only two mechanisms of ATP synthesis: substrate-level and oxidative. ATP synthesis by oxidative pathways is also known as cellular respiration.
